title: Stabilizing controller design and the belgian chocolate problem
contribution: A minlp.org problem-library entry that packages the nonconvex MINLP for stabilizing controller design (up to degree 8) on the open Belgian chocolate problem as a GAMS model.
problem_entry: An open control question used as a global-MINLP test: the exact stabilizability limit delta-bar is unknown and every controller found computationally is a lower bound (best known 0.974, from their own 2007 paper) (p. 1).
key_idea: Stability needs the largest real part of the zeros negative, giving a bilevel minimax program, made single-level by extending their 2004 reformulation for matrix stability; the entry ships the GAMS model (pp. 1-2).
assumptions: Single-parameter process, minimum-phase stable controller, controller degree up to 8; the reformulation is only cited (pp. 1-2).
proof_devices: n/a: no derivation in the two-page entry (pp. 1-2)
positioning: Cites Blondel's theory and the nonsmooth-optimization bounds of Burke, Henrion, Lewis and Overton, and gives its own 2007 bound 0.974 as the best known (pp. 1-2).
writing: Two-page library overview: application motivation, the open question, the best known bound, then the reformulation and what the file provides (pp. 1-2).
limits_future: None stated; no solver results or instance statistics in the entry (pp. 1-2).

method_links.note: step 5: the 2007 paper's model released as a stand-alone GAMS instance in the minlp.org library; whether it entered BARON's development set is not stated

new_pattern_candidates.evidence: a library instance whose solved cases are publishable facts: each certified stabilizing controller improves the best known lower bound (0.974) on the open constant delta-bar

transferable: Release a hard model from a paper as a two-page library entry that states what is open, the best known bound and its source, names the reformulation used, and ships the modeling-language file (pp. 1-2).

quotes.text: Since the stability of a polynomial requires the maximum real part of its zeros to be negative, the stabilizing controller design problem results in a bilevel minimax optimization program.
Here, we provide a GAMS implementation of the nonconvex MINLP for the stabilizing controller design problem for the Belgian chocolate problem using up to degree 8 controllers.

title: Exploiting physical properties in protein structure alignment
contribution: A meeting abstract showing that a secondary-structure-based search-space reduction speeds up the exact alignment code CMOS about five-fold with 0.8% deviation from the optimum, while three other physical features cost too much quality.
problem_entry: Alignment tools use geometry only; physical features are not well understood and unused, so test them inside an exact tool, CMOS (MAX-CMO) (p. 1).
key_idea: Use each physical feature as a search-space reduction in CMOS and measure matches eliminated, deviation from the optimal alignment and speed-up (p. 1).
assumptions: The reductions are heuristic and can cut off the exact optimum, hence the measured deviation; reduction rules and test set are not described in the abstract (Table 1, p. 1).
experiments: Table 1: secondary structures 24% of matches eliminated, 0.8% deviation, 5x speed-up; torsion angles 28%/14%, hydropathy 12%/7%, solvent accessibility 42%/16% (speed-up N.A.); test set not described (p. 1).
positioning: Builds on the authors' exact tool CMOS (Xie and Sahinidis 2007) against geometric-only alignment tools (p. 1).
writing: Standard meeting-abstract structure; the three negative results are stated as plainly as the positive one (p. 1).
limits_future: Hydropathy, torsion angles and solvent accessibility found of little use; no future work stated (p. 1).

method_links.note: reduce the search space before the exact search, carried to proteins in CMOS, but with non-valid reductions priced by share removed, deviation from the exact optimum and speed-up; three of four rejected

transferable: For each candidate pruning rule in an exact algorithm, report the share of the search space removed, the deviation from the exact optimum and the speed-up side by side; adopt only rules with near-zero deviation and publish the rejected ones with their numbers (Table 1, p. 1).

quotes.text: Our computational studies indicate that a search space reduction based on secondary structures leads to an over five-fold reduction in CPU requirements while maintaining solution quality [Table 1].

title: Overview of the US DOE's Carbon Capture Simulation Initiative for Accelerating the Commercialization of CCS Technology
contribution: A consortium programme overview (20 authors, Sahinidis 11th) of the DOE Carbon Capture Simulation Initiative: a toolset built around three industry challenge problems with cross-cutting V&V, multi-scale integration, UQ, optimization and risk analysis.
problem_entry: Capture would add about 80% (pulverized coal) or 35% (gasification) to the cost of electricity and scale-up could take 20-30 years; validated simulation with UQ should allow larger scale-up steps earlier (p. 4).
key_idea: Three industry challenge problems chosen by development-cycle stage (solid sorbents at the start, advanced solvents in the middle, oxy-combustion near the end), one application at a time with reusable common components; ten task sets in three focus areas, Task Set 3 Process Synthesis and Design (pp. 5-8).
assumptions: n/a: programme plan; named simulators FLUENT, Aspen Plus, DYNSIM, MFIX (p. 8).
positioning: Places CCSI inside DOE/NETL's CCS RD&D programme and the 2010 Presidential memorandum, citing aerospace and automotive experience with simulation (p. 4).
writing: Programme prose with enumerated goals (1)-(4) and lists of challenges; no results (pp. 4-9).
limits_future: Five-year plan; industry partners refine the challenge problems and evaluate the toolset; no limits discussed (p. 9).

method_links.note: origin context only: the stated challenge of optimizing large integrated models with quantified uncertainty is the setting SKILL.md gives as ALAMO's origin; no method of Sahinidis's own in the text (consortium voice)

transferable: Pick case studies at different stages of their technology's development (start, middle, end of the development cycle), so that pilot validation data arrive in sequence and each case adds a capability to the same toolset (pp. 5-6).
coauthors: D. C. Miller (corresponding), M. Syamlal, J. C. Meza, D. L. Brown, M. M. Fox, M. A. Khaleel, R. K. Cottrell, J. D. Kress, X. Sun, S. Sundaresan, S. E. Zitney, D. A. Agarwal, C. Tong, G. Lin, B. C. Letellier, D. W. Engel, P. Calafiura, G. A. Richards, J. H. Shinn

quotes.text: The strength of our ICP approach is that it will advance the state of the art by focusing on one concrete application at a time
CCSI will address the challenge of optimizing large-scale integrated models with quantified uncertainties.

title: SAS-Pro: Simultaneous residue assignment and structure superposition for protein structure alignment
contribution: Reformulates protein structure alignment as a bilevel problem with an exact polynomial-time k-cardinality assignment subproblem and a low-dimensional rotation-translation master solved by a benchmark-chosen DFO solver (SNOBFIT), giving sequential and non-sequential alignments in about a CPU minute per pair.
problem_entry: Two-stage tools decouple assignment and superposition and may give suboptimal, initialization-dependent alignments, while exact contact-map tools are expensive; stated as an RMSD-minimizing MINLP (pp. 1-3).
key_idea: Master over theta (6 or 3 degrees of freedom) whose objective is the optimal value of a k-LAP solved exactly by SKAP; no sequentiality constraints; DFO (SNOBFIT, picked from 28 solvers) for the non-algebraic multimodal master; centroids fix translation; r_m scanned automatically (pp. 3-6).
assumptions: Rigid C-alpha backbones (p. 2); similar proteins align 85-100% of the smaller one (pp. 4-5); centroid coincidence approximates translation for similar sizes (p. 5); no bond rotations (p. 9).
proof_devices: equivalence of the bilevel reformulation: every MINLP-feasible point is master-feasible and one objective at both levels makes a SAS-Pro optimum an MINLP optimum (pp. 3-4)
SRMSD(theta) = sqrt(k_theta/r_m) from the k-LAP value (p. 4)
dynamic program extracting the largest sequential alignment (pp. 5-6)
no proof of master optimality: budgeted SNOBFIT, result called near-optimal (p. 4)
experiments: 850 Sokol/Skolnick pairs and 23 RIPC problems, about 1 CPU min per pair; 96% agreement with exact CMOS, RMSD better or equal on 59-69% of similar pairs vs CE/SSM/STSA, perfect classification at SAS 4 A; RIPC mean/median 62%/70%, below STSA but 8 vs 4 perfect matches; most competitor figures copied from [33] (pp. 6-8).
positioning: Recasts two-stage tools (Structal, MAMMOTH, Andreani et al.) as a decomposition that loses optimality and separates SAS-Pro from Kolodny and Linial's bilevel scheme on three points: same objective at both levels, search instead of grid enumeration, non-sequential capability (pp. 2-4).
writing: The abstract's claim of better RMSD and longer alignments is broader than the tables (better or equal on 59-69%; STSA ahead on RIPC mean and median), and losses are explained by possible alternative alignments (pp. 1, 6-9).
limits_future: Future work: bond-rotation degrees of freedom (p. 9); global optimality of the master not guaranteed (p. 4); three RIPC problems below 50% agreement, said to have possible alternative alignments (p. 9).

method_links.note: step 7: 28 DFO solvers tested and SNOBFIT chosen at the affordable budget, consistent with the Rios-Sahinidis benchmark, whose result on 3-4-variable problems justifies cutting the master to three angles; the SNOBFIT interface is based on Rios's in-house 'mydfo'
step 7: DFO used only for the few continuous degrees of freedom with no algebraic form; the combinatorial part stays an exact polynomial-time subproblem

competitor figures copied from [33] rather than rerun (only CE rerun); the 4 A cutoff read off the Skolnick results is built into the r_m scan and stopping rule, so the classification claim is in-sample
the master's space is shrunk before search (translation fixed by centroids) by an approximation that holds very often, not by a valid inference

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: exact inner subproblem, derivative-free outer master
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: MINLP split into an exactly solvable combinatorial k-LAP subproblem and a low-dimensional black-box master over rotation-translation, with one objective at both levels

transferable: Split a mixed-integer alignment or registration problem into a polynomial-time exact subproblem for the discrete part and a low-dimensional continuous master, with one objective at both levels so a global master optimum is a global MINLP optimum (pp. 3-4).

Before choosing a black-box solver for a new application, test an existing DFO benchmark's candidates at the budget the application allows, and cut the master's dimension into the range where the benchmark shows solvers reliably reach global optima (pp. 4-5).
Let the code set its own key parameter by a scan with a quality-based stop (r_m from 100% to 85% of the smaller protein, stop at SASnseq < 4 A) (pp. 4-6).
Where an exact method exists for part of the test set, measure the heuristic's agreement with the exact optima (96% with CMOS) (p. 6).

quotes.text: Global optimality cannot be guaranteed unless the MINLP is somehow solved directly.

We performed extensive computational analysis with 28 different DFO solvers, based on a variety of techniques that included direct search, pattern search, surrogate management frameworks, domain partitioning methods, local search, global search, deterministic and stochastic algorithms [37].

title: Computational tools for accelerating carbon capture process development
contribution: An 18-slide 2013 progress talk on the CCSI process-synthesis chain: ALAMO algebraic surrogates of rigorous simulations, superstructure optimization for the configuration, simulation-based optimization to verify it, and UQ, with the toolset released in October 2012.
problem_entry: Accelerate carbon capture development: identify promising concepts, cut design and troubleshooting time, quantify technical risk, stabilize deployment cost (p. 1).
key_idea: Process models -> algebraic surrogates (ALAMO: 14 inputs, >900 possible terms, 0.13% error, terms labelled physically) -> superstructure optimization -> simulation-based optimization that verifies the solution -> UQ (pp. 2, 4-6).
assumptions: Explicit lower and upper bounds on every decision variable (p. 7); model equations not in the text layer.
experiments: One case: optimized solid-sorbent process 2.79 GJ per tonne CO2 vs 3.44 and 2.90 for two MEA27 configurations; no test set or protocol (p. 7).
positioning: Places the tools inside the CCSI toolset and its release plan (pp. 2, 9).
writing: Slide deck in which one example model with physically annotated terms carries the ALAMO message (p. 4).
limits_future: Releases planned for 2013-2015, final release January 2016; no limits stated (p. 9).

method_links.note: steps 3, 6, 7: simple algebraic surrogates of rigorous simulations, terms read physically, embedded in a superstructure optimization

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: surrogate picks the configuration, rigorous simulation verifies it
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: superstructure optimization on ALAMO surrogates chooses the configuration; simulation-based optimization on the rigorous model then verifies the solution (also S347 pp. 11, 19)

transferable: When presenting a learned surrogate, label each selected term with its physical meaning so the audience can judge whether the model makes sense (p. 4).
Use algebraic surrogates to choose the configuration in a superstructure, then verify and refine that configuration by simulation-based optimization on the rigorous model (pp. 2, 5-6).
coauthors: D. C. Miller, A. Cozad, A. Lee, H. Kim, J. Morinelly, J. Eslick, Z. Yuan

quotes.text: For building accurate, simple algebraic surrogate models of simulated processes
Initial toolset released Oct. 2012, 1 year ahead of schedule due to industry request for early access

title: Annual Report: Carbon Capture Simulation Initiative
contribution: The CCSI FY12 annual report (16 names, Sahinidis 7th and co-lead of Process Synthesis & Design), documenting the first ALAMO release with MIP best-subset selection and error-maximization sampling packaged beside lasso, least squares and Latin hypercube baselines.
problem_entry: CCSI goals as in S217; a first toolset pre-release came a year ahead of plan because of industry interest (p. 10).
key_idea: Element 3 released process models, system examples and three optimization tools (ALAMO; a superstructure on algebraic surrogates for the configuration; simulation-based optimization for a given configuration), with ALAMO in Matlab and stand-alone Windows versions and five input modes (pp. 11, 18-20).
assumptions: n/a for ALAMO (no model statements); moving-bed model with automatic homotopy initialization (p. 19).
experiments: No ALAMO results; re-optimized MEA benchmark at a best cost of electricity of $114/MWh (p. 19); water-network Lagrangean algorithm said to improve solution time without numbers (p. 20).
positioning: Programme report; Element 3 lists tools and talks without positioning against other surrogate tools (pp. 18-21).
writing: Accomplishment lists per element, each closing with the same mission sentence and the IAB-review sentence (e.g. pp. 21, 24, 27).
limits_future: No limits stated for ALAMO; other elements note that ROMs need many CFD runs and simulator licences block massively parallel runs (p. 27); plans for Feb 2013-Jan 2014 under review (p. 21).

method_links.note: the first release packaged both published components (MIP best subset, error-maximization sampling) as ALAMO's standard methods; the report does not say which sampler was the default, which bears on SKILL.md's say-do note on adaptive sampling
step 4 analogue in a surrogate tool: lasso, least squares and Latin hypercube ship beside the method's components so each can be switched off in one code; no such comparison shown

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: surrogate picks the configuration, rigorous simulation verifies it
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: superstructure on algebraic surrogates for the configuration and simulation-based optimization for design and operating conditions of a given configuration are released as separate tools (also S173 pp. 2, 6)

transferable: Ship the standard baselines inside your tool next to the new components (lasso and least squares beside best-subset MIP; Latin hypercube beside adaptive sampling), so any user can run the comparison (pp. 19-20).

Accept several input modes (fixed data set, pre-run sample, tool-guided design of experiments, script or executable simulator wrapper), so the same surrogate builder works whether or not the user can call the simulator (p. 20).

quotes.text: Packaged with the ALAMO suite are several modeling methods: the standard ALAMO model builder mixed integer problem best-subset method, the lasso regularization, and ordinary least squares regression.
The adaptive sampling routines available include the standard ALAMO error maximization sampling method as well as Latin hypercube sampling.

title: Uncertainty Quantification in CO2 Sequestration Using Surrogate Models from Polynomial Chaos Expansion
contribution: Builds sparse polynomial chaos surrogates of a TOUGH2 CO2-storage simulator by best-subset MIP with cross-validated size, validates the UQ against 1000 direct simulations, and optimizes the injection rate under uncertainty with BARON.
problem_entry: Monte Carlo on detailed simulators is too costly and full PCE needs as many simulations as terms; collocation PCE assumed parametric distributions rejected for the same data, and stepwise selection ignores synergistic terms (pp. 3-4, 9-10).
key_idea: min ||B alpha - y||^2 with sum w_j = T and alpha bounds switched by binaries, T chosen by leave-one-out Q2, inside a degree-raising loop; Nataf transform for correlated empirical inputs; the design variable enters as a uniform input and the scenario problem is solved globally with BARON (pp. 7, 9-12, 28-29).
assumptions: Finite-variance outputs (p. 5); fixed 100-point LHS design ordered by density (pp. 8, 16); two correlated inputs from field data (p. 15); TOUGH2 Problem 4 on 986 blocks (pp. 14-15, 18); injection rate uniform in 0.5-1.5 times base, pressure limit 4e7 Pa (p. 28); coefficient bounds unstated (p. 10).
proof_devices: cardinality-constrained best-subset MIP with cross-validated cardinality (p. 10)
Dvoretzky-Kiefer-Wolfowitz inequality to set 1000 Monte Carlo samples (p. 22)
sample-average scenario problem P2 over 1000 realizations and per-scenario problems P3, solved with BARON (p. 29)
experiments: CDFs from third- and fourth-order surrogates very close to 1000 direct TOUGH2 runs at about 10% of the cost (pp. 22-24); MIP simpler than stepwise on 93.9% of 904 outputs at similar Q2, more terms on 6.10% (pp. 19, 21-22); 89 of 239 saturation PCEs negative, clipped to zero (p. 19); overpressure probability 0.17 at fixed rate (p. 29).
positioning: Against collocation PCE with parametric inputs (Oladyshkin et al., with Kopp et al.'s test) and stepwise sparse PCE (Blatman and Sudret); extends Oladyshkin's integrative design-variable idea to optimization (pp. 4, 9-11).
writing: Two numbered contributions (pp. 4-5); strong closing claims: 'Clearly then' fewer simulations (not measured, p. 21) and 'a rigorous way' to set the injection rate (pp. 30, 32).
limits_future: Contour wiggles and negative saturations from polynomial oscillation (p. 19); two uncertain inputs (p. 15); the fewer-simulations claim untested since both methods used the same 100 runs (pp. 21, 23); no future work stated.

method_links.note: steps 3, 6, 7: smallest accurate basis subset by integer programming with cross-validated size; fitted surface read physically; surrogate optimized globally with BARON
steps 4, 5: the physical bound (saturation >= 0) is applied after fitting by clipping, not imposed during fitting, and sampling is a fixed density-ordered LHS design, not adaptive

yardstick is brute-force truth (1000 direct simulations) rather than a certified optimum; the rival is the standard method at an equal simulation budget over all 904 outputs, with the losing share reported

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: design variable as a uniform random input of the surrogate
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: the injection rate enters the PCE as a uniform random variable, so one surrogate serves both UQ and the design optimization solved with BARON

transferable: Replace forward/backward stepwise term selection by a cardinality-constrained best-subset MIP, choose the cardinality by leave-one-out Q2, and raise the degree until Q2 stops improving (pp. 9-12).
Compare with the standard method at the same simulation budget and target accuracy on every output, and tabulate where the new method loses (Table 1, pp. 21-22).
Before trusting a surrogate-based UQ pipeline, validate it once against brute-force Monte Carlo on a case where the simulator is still affordable (pp. 22-24).
Size the Monte Carlo sample with the Dvoretzky-Kiefer-Wolfowitz bound instead of a rule of thumb (p. 22).
Use empirical marginals from field data plus a Nataf transformation for correlated inputs instead of fitting parametric distributions (pp. 7, 15).

quotes.text: To cope with this limitation, instead of using a classical full expansion at each step of an iterative PCE construction method, we introduce a mixed-integer programming (MIP) formulation to identify the best subset of basis terms in the expansion.

We conclude that 93.9% of the time the MIP-based method performs better than forward and backward stepwise regression in the sense that it yields simpler models based on the same number of simulations.

title: Developing Surrogate Models for CO2 Sequestration Using Polynomial Chaos Expansion
contribution: An NRAP agency-report restatement of S052's best-subset MIP polynomial chaos surrogates for CO2 storage, without the optimization part and with an executive summary that claims more than the body shows.
problem_entry: As in S052: Monte Carlo on TOUGH2-type simulators is too costly and full PCE needs at least N_t simulations (pp. 10-12).
key_idea: Same best-subset MIP in the degree-raising loop, here named 'MIP-based stepwise regression' (Fig. 2, p. 13), with a new R2/Q2-versus-T figure that picks T at the Q2 maximum (Fig. 3, p. 14).
assumptions: Two inputs for illustration (p. 15); the benchmark is said to be based on a project of about one million tons of CO2 a year (p. 15), while S052 gives about 10 kilotons a year; not reconciled.
proof_devices: n/a: details referred to Zhang and Sahinidis 2013 (pp. 11-14)
experiments: 100 LHS samples, example R2 = Q2 = 0.98 (p. 17); 1000 TOUGH2 runs for validation, PCE run under 0.1 s, total about 10% of direct Monte Carlo, second-order surrogate CDF very close to TOUGH2 (pp. 18-19).
positioning: Refers to Zhang and Sahinidis 2013 for all details and positions against stepwise PCE (Blatman and Sudret) (pp. 11-12).
writing: Agency-report format with an executive summary that claims a SACROC application and a 6% maximum relative error not shown in the body (p. 9).
limits_future: No future work stated; the SACROC application and the 6% maximum relative error of the summary (p. 9) are not supported in the body (pp. 9-20), and S052 gives 6% as the average size of negative-saturation errors (S052 p. 19).

method_links.note: restatement of S052's best-subset MIP surrogate with cross-validated size and brute-force validation

transferable: Plot training R2 and leave-one-out Q2 against the number of terms T in one figure and take T at the Q2 maximum (Fig. 3, p. 14).

quotes.text: The technique has been applied to simulations of a 2-D benchmark problem and the Scurry Area Canyon Reef Operators Committee (SACROC) oilfield.
The resulting maximum relative error for the benchmark problem is 6%.
